description: Ask a database for exactly what you want: pick columns with SELECT, pick the table with FROM, filter rows with WHERE.

screens.body:
Every example in this track uses the same small table called students. Think of it like a spreadsheet: columns are id, name, program, and gpa — and it holds six students.

Memorize the shape, not the rows: a table is rows (each student) and columns (each fact about them). Everything SQL does starts from this picture.

check.question: A database table is made of…

code.snippet:
-- the students table (6 rows, 4 columns)
-- id | name     | program              | gpa
--  1 | Morolake | Software Development | 3.8
--  2 | Tega     | Network Security     | 3.2
--  3 | Ama      | Software Development | 2.9
--  4 | Liam     | Data Science         | 3.6
--  5 | Priya    | Software Development | 3.9
--  6 | Noah     | Network Security     | 2.4

screens.heading: Your sample data: the students table
screens.keyPoint: A table is rows and columns — that's the whole starting picture.

screens.body:
SELECT names the columns you want back. It never touches the table — it just chooses what to show you.

SELECT name, program says 'show me the name and program columns, nothing else.' Want everything? Use the star: SELECT * means all columns.

options: Only the name and program columns
The whole table no matter what
check.question: SELECT name, program FROM students shows…

screens.heading: SELECT picks the columns
screens.keyPoint: SELECT decides which columns come back.

screens.body:
FROM tells SQL where to look. SELECT picks the columns, FROM picks the table they live in.

Read it as a sentence: 'SELECT name FROM students' = 'give me the name column from the students table.' You always need both halves — one without the other is a broken sentence.
screens.heading: FROM picks the table
screens.keyPoint: SELECT names the columns; FROM names the table.

screens.body:
WHERE keeps only the rows that match a condition. SELECT name FROM students WHERE gpa >= 3.5 returns the names of students whose GPA is 3.5 or higher — Morolake, Liam, and Priya.

The operators are the ones you know: = , > , < , >= , <=. The table stays untouched; you just get a smaller answer.

options: Only rows that pass the condition
The highest GPA as a number
check.question: WHERE gpa >= 3.5 returns…

code.snippet:
SELECT name
FROM students
WHERE gpa >= 3.5;
-- returns: Morolake, Liam, Priya

screens.heading: WHERE filters the rows
screens.keyPoint: WHERE keeps only rows that pass the test.

screens.body:
The three clauses go in a fixed order: SELECT, then FROM, then WHERE. Read it top to bottom: 'SELECT name (what) FROM students (where) WHERE program = 'Software Development' (which ones).'

That order never changes. The database reads it in a different order behind the scenes, but you always WRITE it this way.

options: SELECT name FROM students WHERE program = 'Data Science';
FROM students SELECT name WHERE program = 'Data Science';
WHERE program = 'Data Science' FROM students SELECT name;
check.question: Which query is written correctly?

code.snippet:
SELECT name
FROM students
WHERE program = 'Software Development';
-- returns: Morolake, Ama, Priya

screens.heading: SQL reads like a sentence
screens.keyPoint: SELECT → FROM → WHERE, always in that order.

screens.body:
Text values go in single quotes: WHERE name = 'Liam'. Numbers stay bare: WHERE gpa > 3.0. Mix them up and the query breaks.

It's the same habit as JavaScript: strings need quotes, numbers don't. Capitalization of keywords (SELECT vs select) doesn't matter, but uppercase is the convention.
screens.heading: Text needs quotes, numbers don't
screens.keyPoint: Strings in single quotes, numbers bare.

screens.body:
A query never changes the table — SELECT, WHERE, and friends are read-only. You can't break anything by reading.

In this track's exercises, you'll prove each SQL idea with JavaScript: the same dataset as an array, the same result with filter() and map(). Read in SQL, do in JavaScript — the logic is the same.

screens.heading: One more idea before practice
screens.keyPoint: SELECT never changes the table — reading is always safe.
